prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the physiology and active molecular form of glucagon-like peptide-1 that made incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: All six opening ballots place B046 first, and I do not treat that unanimity as proof of merit. The merit rests on the discovery itself. GLP-1 secretion, its insulinotropic and satiety actions, and the identification of the active truncated peptide form are original physiological findings. They were converted, through decades of independent work and large randomised outcome trials, into a therapeutic class with documented cardiovascular, renal and weight benefits. The chain from hormone biology to patient outcome is complete, the evidence is mature, and the timing is pressing because clinical impact is already very large. A single-achievement prize built on the physiological discovery (Holst, Drucker, Mojsov) is coherent and keeps the citation tied to what was discovered rather than to a product.
statement.case_against: The credit is the weakest point. Mojsov's priority over the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is contested, and I have not verified it from the supplied evidence. Habener and others are not on the credited list. Excluding Knudsen, who led the engineering of long-acting liraglutide and semaglutide, can be read as honouring the discovery while leaving out the people who produced the medicine. If the committee considers drug development essential to the achievement, a three-name physiology prize is incomplete. Separately, CAR-T (B028) is the other candidate with a similarly clear bench-to-bedside arc and has not been honoured, so a one-part GLP-1 prize leaves a strong therapeutic achievement unrewarded this year.

responses.point: As chair, Svenningsson proposed Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, treating Knudsen as the pharmaceutical design of long-acting analogues in place of Mojsov, whose early characterisation of the active peptide he described as contested.
responses.response: I take the point that the contested Mojsov priority is a real risk, and I agree the allocation is not clean. I still prefer Mojsov to Knudsen for a prize about what was discovered. The identification and synthesis of the active peptide is the molecular step that made GLP-1 usable as a hormone and a target, whereas Knudsen's contribution is the medicinal chemistry of half-life extension, which is excellent engineering but a later stage. I would revisit this if the committee decides the citation should name the medicines. In that case Knudsen would have a strong claim, and the question would be whether she should displace Drucker or Holst. I do not think she should.

responses.point: Linnarsson called Knudsen's role real but industrial engineering of the drug, and flagged priority disputes over who first identified the active GLP-1(7-36) form. He also ranked CAR-T second, ahead of optogenetics and cGAS-STING.
responses.response: I agree with his reading of Knudsen. His priority concern is the one I share, and the open question is whether it can be settled from the evidence we have. If it cannot, I would rather cite the physiological discovery and name the peptide chemistry modestly than leave out Mojsov on an unverified claim. On CAR-T I am closer to him than the ranking suggests: it is my clear second choice, and I would pair it with GLP-1 only if the committee wants a two-part prize.

responses.point: Perlmann ranked cGAS-STING second, reasoning that cytosolic DNA sensing defines a new innate-immune axis with implications for infection, autoimmunity and cancer, and proposed Chen and Barber, with a possible third from the co-discoverers.
responses.response: This is the colleague I most want to engage. I rank cGAS-STING fourth, and as an autoimmunity researcher I find the pathway compelling. Human genetic disease (STING-associated vasculopathy, Aicardi-Goutieres syndrome, lupus-like phenotypes) confirms its relevance. But there is no approved therapy yet, so the case today is mechanistic. I think the prize is better served by waiting for clinical validation than by giving the pathway a prize on conceptual strength alone. I also do not accept a possible third name from the co-discoverers. Ishikawa's STING priority claim against Barber is unresolved, and adding a name would not fix that.

responses.point: Sandberg ranked antisense SMN2 correction (B007) second and CAR-T third, and described Knudsen's work as translational and a better fit for a separate recognition than for the physiology prize.
responses.response: I agree about Knudsen, and I have less certainty about B007 than he does. Nusinersen is a clean mechanism-to-drug story with a clear credit pair, so I would not rate it below cGAS-STING on attribution. But the breadth is narrower, and the prize would honour a single disease and an RNA-therapeutic platform whose wider impact is still developing. I rank it sixth. The SMN1 gene discovery by Melki and Lefebvre is also outside the credit, which weakens a prize framed as the full arc.

uncertainties: Whether Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide can be settled from the evidence supplied, and whether Habener should be considered.
Whether the committee wants the citation to cover the physiological discovery or the drug development, which decides if Knudsen should replace one of the three names.
Whether a one-part GLP-1 prize is preferable to a two-part prize that adds CAR-T (B028), given that Eshhar is outside the credit and Rosenberg's work is broader than CARs.
Long-term safety and central mechanisms of GLP-1 agonists remain under study.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for any shortlisted candidate. The co-authors recorded in my profile (Vijay Kuchroo, Sven-Erik Sonesson) are not credited names on any shortlisted ballot. My expertise in autoimmunity is relevant to cGAS-STING and CAR-T, but that is a scientific perspective and not a personal or institutional tie.
